nlmixr2bayes and Torsten

Source: vignettes/torsten-comparison.Rmd
torsten-comparison.Rmd

Torsten (Metrum Research Group) and nlmixr2bayes both bring Stan’s NUTS sampler to pharmacometric models, from opposite directions:

  • Torsten is a library of Stan functions (pmx_solve_onecpt, pmx_solve_twocpt, pmx_solve_linode, pmx_solve_rk45/bdf/adams, coupled PK-forced-PD solvers) with NONMEM-convention event handling (AMT/EVID/CMT/RATE/ADDL/II/SS). You write the full Stan program by hand: data block, parameter transforms, the eta hierarchy, the residual model, generated quantities. Total control, and total responsibility.

  • nlmixr2bayes is a full nlmixr2 estimation method: the model is the same ini({})/model({}) function every other nlmixr2 method fits, the Stan program is generated, and Stan is linked to the compiled rxode2/nlmixr2est likelihood (with analytic gradients) rather than the model being re-expressed in Stan’s language. The fit comes back as a standard nlmixr2FitData with GOF tables, plus the full stanfit. For programs you write yourself, the same package also ships the rxstan bridge (vignette("rxstan-handcoded", "nlmixr2bayes")): Torsten-style hand-written Stan, but with rxode2 as the solver instead of Stan’s own ode_* functions or Torsten’s pmx_solve_*.

The practical consequence: a Torsten model is ~100-200 lines of Stan; the same model in nlmixr2bayes is the ~20-line nlmixr2 function you may already have from a FOCEi/SAEM run, and the posterior is sampled against the identical likelihood code those methods used.

Capability comparison

capability Torsten nlmixr2bayes
1/2-cmt analytic models pmx_solve_onecpt/twocpt linCmt() (1/2/3-cmt + absorption)
general linear ODE matrix exponential (pmx_solve_linode) rxode2 solvers
general (stiff) ODE pmx_solve_rk45/bdf/adams rxode2 (lsoda/liblsoda/dop853, …)
delay differential equations – rxode2 delay() / past(), through both the automatic est="stan" path and the rxstan hand-coded bridge
NONMEM-convention events (AMT/EVID/ADDL/SS/RATE) yes yes (rxode2 event table)
estimated alag/f/dur/rate parameters of the solve (Torsten notes an open adjoint issue at tlag = 0) yes; jump-condition sensitivities, FD-verified
residual models hand-written (anything Stan can express) nlmixr2 catalog (add/prop/combined, lnorm, …), censoring M2/M3/M4, user ll()
eta structure hand-written (any structure, incl. IOV by hand) lotri blocks; non-centered or centered; fixed-variance etas (constant Cholesky factor); first-class IOV (iov.x ~ v \| OCC through nlmixr2est’s iov hook: per-occasion fixed unit-variance etas scaled by an estimated magnitude theta, FD-verified)
finite mixtures hand-written mix() (2 components): log-sum-exp marginalization, membership posteriors in fit$env$mixProb
priors any Stan distribution, hand-written the 39-distribution lotri catalog via prior() in ini({}), LKJ/inv-Wishart on omega
single-subject (no etas) yes yes (“tier 0”: the nlm path’s likelihood + analytic theta gradients, one external scalar nlmixr2_pop_ll(theta))
gradients Stan autodiff through the solvers analytic forward sensitivities via precomputed_gradients
within-chain parallelism MPI (map_rect-style population solvers) subject-parallel OpenMP inside each likelihood evaluation (cores)
interface cmdstan / cmdstanr rstan, nlmixr2(..., est = "stan")
output cmdstan CSV; roll your own diagnostics/GOF nlmixr2FitData (IPRED/CWRES tables, $objDf with FOCEi/WAIC/LOO rows) + the stanfit
model reuse across estimation methods Stan-only the same function fits with focei/saem/bobyqa/…

Where Torsten is the right tool: hand-tuned Stan programs, structures outside the nlmixr2 ui (e.g. exotic hierarchies), and cmdstan-ecosystem workflows. Where nlmixr2bayes is the right tool: standard population PK/PD where the model already exists in nlmixr2 form, and the Bayesian run should be comparable line-for-line with the frequentist ones.

There is also a middle ground: an rxode2 sensitivity linkage for hand-written Stan programs (the rxstan bridge covered in vignette("rxstan-handcoded", "nlmixr2bayes")) – write your own Stan code (any hierarchy, any prior structure) while the ODE system, dosing events, and their analytic sensitivities come from a compiled rxode2 model (including event-time “jump” sensitivities and delay differential equations, which no Stan-native solver provides). It shares the same no-Stan-code-in-the-linked-.so architecture as the automatic path, just at the ODE level instead of the likelihood level.

How the ports below are checked

Each port is a real nlmixr2 model, and each one is put through est = "stan" code generation with run = FALSE – which builds the complete Stan program and its data list without touching the sampler – and the result is handed to rstan::stanc(). A program that stanc accepts is a program that would have compiled and sampled; that is what keeps these ports honest without needing cmdstan and Torsten installed. (The same checks run in the package’s own test-torsten-port.R.)

library(nlmixr2)
library(nlmixr2bayes)

## generate the Stan program for a model + data, and assert stanc accepts it
portCheck <- function(model, data) {
  code <- nlmixr2est::nlmixr2(model, data, est = "stan",
                              control = stanControl(run = FALSE))
  stopifnot(rstan::stanc(model_code = code$code,
                         allow_undefined = TRUE)$status)
  code
}

The datasets below are small synthetic event tables in the NONMEM convention, enough to exercise generation. Sampling-level agreement with Torsten itself would need cmdstan plus Torsten’s own example data; see “A note on completeness” at the end.

Port: poppk2cpt (two-compartment population model)

Torsten’s example-models/poppk2cpt is ~150 lines of Stan: NONMEM-style arrays in data, pmx_solve_twocpt per subject, Matt’s trick (Matt Hoffman) for the etas, lognormal priors, lognormal residual. The same model in nlmixr2bayes:

poppk2cpt <- function() {
  ini({
    lcl <- log(10)
    lq <- log(15)
    lv1 <- log(35)
    lv2 <- log(105)
    lka <- log(2.5)
    # Torsten's lognormal priors on the natural scale are normal priors on
    # the log-scale parameters
    prior(lcl) ~ dnorm(log(10), 0.25)
    prior(lq) ~ dnorm(log(15), 0.5)
    prior(lv1) ~ dnorm(log(35), 0.25)
    prior(lv2) ~ dnorm(log(105), 0.5)
    prior(lka) ~ dnorm(log(2.5), 1)
    lnorm.sd <- c(0, 0.2)
    prior(lnorm.sd) ~ dcauchy(0, 1)
    # IIV block; the default omega prior is announced as
    # lkj_corr_cholesky(2) + half-Cauchy SDs -- the same shape Torsten's
    # examples hand-code
    eta.cl + eta.q + eta.v1 + eta.v2 + eta.ka ~
      c(0.06,
        0.01, 0.06,
        0.01, 0.01, 0.06,
        0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.06,
        0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.06)
  })
  model({
    cl <- exp(lcl + eta.cl)
    q <- exp(lq + eta.q)
    v <- exp(lv1 + eta.v1)    # central volume (Torsten's V1)
    vp <- exp(lv2 + eta.v2)   # peripheral volume (Torsten's V2)
    ka <- exp(lka + eta.ka)
    # pmx_solve_twocpt's analytic solution == linCmt() with these params
    cp <- linCmt()
    # logCObs ~ normal(log(cHat), sigma) == a lognormal residual
    cp ~ lnorm(lnorm.sd)
  })
}

The event table is the same NONMEM-convention data both tools consume – no iObs/start/end index bookkeeping; rxode2 derives it:

d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, function(id) {
  rbind(data.frame(ID = id, TIME = 0, DV = NA_real_, AMT = 1000, EVID = 1),
        data.frame(ID = id, TIME = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24),
                   DV = c(20, 25, 18, 10, 6, 2), AMT = 0, EVID = 0))
}))
codePop <- portCheck(poppk2cpt, d)

A real run is then nlmixr2(poppk2cpt, d, est = "nuts"). The generated program is what it would sample; the correlated five-eta block is where Torsten’s hand-coded Matt’s trick shows up, emitted rather than written:

cat(grep("Lcorr|lkj|^\\s*z\\b|eta\\[|matrix", strsplit(codePop$code, "\n")[[1]],
         value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
#>   vector nlmixr2_cond_all2(matrix etaMat, vector theta);
#>   cholesky_factor_corr[5] Lcorr_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka;
#>   matrix[N, 5] z_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka;
#>   matrix[N, 5] eta;
#>   theta[1] = lcl;
#>   theta[2] = lq;
#>   theta[3] = lv1;
#>   theta[4] = lv2;
#>   theta[5] = lka;
#>   theta[6] = lnorm_sd;
#>   matrix[5,5] L_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka = diag_pre_multiply(sd_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka, Lcorr_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka);
#>   eta[, 1:5] = z_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka * L_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka';
#>   Lcorr_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
#>       matrix[5,5] Od_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka = L_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka * L_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka';
#>   matrix[5,5] omegaOut = rep_matrix(0, 5,5);

A note on the eta parameterization: nlmixr2bayes’s generated program uses the same Matt’s trick Torsten’s examples hand-code – by default the etas are non-centered, with z ~ std_normal() sampled and eta = z * L' assembled from the omega Cholesky factor in transformed parameters – it is just emitted for you rather than written by hand. stanControl(etaParam = "centered") switches to the centered form (eta[i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(0, L)); the two are verified to target the identical posterior.

codeCentered <- nlmixr2est::nlmixr2(
  poppk2cpt, d, est = "stan",
  control = stanControl(run = FALSE, etaParam = "centered"))
cat(grep("multi_normal_cholesky|std_normal",
         strsplit(codeCentered$code, "\n")[[1]], value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
#>   for (i in 1:N) etaP_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka[i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(rep_vector(0, 5), L_eta_cl_eta_q_eta_v1_eta_v2_eta_ka);

Port: Friberg-Karlsson neutropenia (population PK/PD, two endpoints)

Torsten’s FribergKarlsson example: a two-compartment PK driving the classic proliferation/transit/circulation myelosuppression chain, ~200 lines with a hand-written 8-state ODE function and separate PK/PD observation indexing. In nlmixr2 syntax:

fk <- function() {
  ini({
    lcl <- log(10); lq <- log(15); lv1 <- log(35); lv2 <- log(105)
    lka <- log(2)
    lmtt <- log(125)
    lcirc0 <- log(5)
    lalpha <- log(3e-4)
    lgamma <- log(0.17)
    prior(lcl) ~ dnorm(log(10), 0.25)
    prior(lmtt) ~ dnorm(log(125), 0.25)
    prior(lcirc0) ~ dnorm(log(5), 0.25)
    prior(lalpha) ~ dnorm(log(3e-4), 1)
    prior(lgamma) ~ dnorm(log(0.17), 0.5)
    lnorm.sd <- c(0, 0.2)
    lnormNeut.sd <- c(0, 0.3)
    prior(lnorm.sd) ~ dcauchy(0, 1)
    prior(lnormNeut.sd) ~ dcauchy(0, 1)
    eta.cl ~ 0.06
    eta.mtt ~ 0.04
    eta.circ0 ~ 0.04
  })
  model({
    cl <- exp(lcl + eta.cl)
    q <- exp(lq); v1 <- exp(lv1); v2 <- exp(lv2); ka <- exp(lka)
    mtt <- exp(lmtt + eta.mtt)
    circ0 <- exp(lcirc0 + eta.circ0)
    alpha <- exp(lalpha)
    gamma <- exp(lgamma)
    k10 <- cl / v1; k12 <- q / v1; k21 <- q / v2
    ktr <- 4 / mtt
    d/dt(depot) <- -ka * depot
    d/dt(cent) <- ka * depot - (k10 + k12) * cent + k21 * peri
    d/dt(peri) <- k12 * cent - k21 * peri
    conc <- cent / v1
    edrug <- alpha * conc
    d/dt(prol) <- ktr * prol * (1 - edrug) * (circ0 / circ)^gamma - ktr * prol
    d/dt(tr1) <- ktr * (prol - tr1)
    d/dt(tr2) <- ktr * (tr1 - tr2)
    d/dt(tr3) <- ktr * (tr2 - tr3)
    d/dt(circ) <- ktr * tr3 - ktr * circ
    prol(0) <- circ0; tr1(0) <- circ0; tr2(0) <- circ0; tr3(0) <- circ0
    circ(0) <- circ0
    # two endpoints, distinguished by CMT/DVID in the data -- Torsten does
    # this with separate iObsPK/iObsPD index arrays
    conc ~ lnorm(lnorm.sd)
    circ ~ lnorm(lnormNeut.sd)
  })
}

The two endpoints are told apart by CMT, and nothing else about the data changes:

dFk <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(id) {
  rbind(data.frame(ID = id, TIME = 0, DV = NA_real_, AMT = 80, EVID = 1,
                   CMT = "depot"),
        data.frame(ID = id, TIME = c(1, 4, 12, 24),
                   DV = c(1.5, 1.1, 0.5, 0.2), AMT = 0, EVID = 0,
                   CMT = "conc"),
        data.frame(ID = id, TIME = c(24, 96, 168, 336),
                   DV = c(4.9, 3.2, 2.1, 4.4), AMT = 0, EVID = 0,
                   CMT = "circ"))
}))
codeFk <- portCheck(fk, dFk)

Multi-endpoint likelihoods, initial conditions, and the stiff ODE solve are all standard rxode2/nlmixr2est machinery; likInner0 sums the per-endpoint terms and the analytic gradients flow through the same linkage. None of that shows up in the Stan program, which is the point – the whole 8-state system, both residual models and both endpoints reduce to one external call:

cat(grep("nlmixr2_cond_all2|^\\s*(vector|matrix|real|array)",
         strsplit(codeFk$code, "\n")[[1]], value = TRUE)[1:12], sep = "\n")
#>   vector nlmixr2_cond_all2(matrix etaMat, vector theta);
#>   real nlmixr2_iter_tick(vector par, real objf);
#>   real lcl;
#>   real lq;
#>   real lv1;
#>   real lv2;
#>   real lka;
#>   real lmtt;
#>   real lcirc0;
#>   real lalpha;
#>   real lgamma;
#>   real<lower=0> lnorm_sd;

Port: effCpt (effect-compartment population PK/PD)

Torsten’s effCpt example: a two-compartment oral PK linked to an effect compartment (ke0) driving an Emax response, fit to concentration and response observations simultaneously (~250 lines of Stan with a hand-built rate matrix and separate PK/PD indexing):

effCpt <- function() {
  ini({
    lcl <- log(10); lq <- log(15); lv1 <- log(35); lv2 <- log(105)
    lka <- log(2)
    lke0 <- log(1)
    lec50 <- log(100)
    prior(lcl) ~ dnorm(log(10), 0.25)
    prior(lke0) ~ dnorm(log(1), 0.25)
    prior(lec50) ~ dnorm(log(100), 0.5)
    lnorm.sd <- c(0, 0.2)
    resp.sd <- c(0, 5)
    prior(lnorm.sd) ~ dcauchy(0, 1)
    prior(resp.sd) ~ dcauchy(0, 5)
    eta.cl ~ 0.06
    eta.v1 ~ 0.06
    eta.ke0 ~ 0.04
    eta.ec50 ~ 0.04
  })
  model({
    cl <- exp(lcl + eta.cl)
    q <- exp(lq)
    v1 <- exp(lv1 + eta.v1)
    v2 <- exp(lv2)
    ka <- exp(lka)
    ke0 <- exp(lke0 + eta.ke0)
    ec50 <- exp(lec50 + eta.ec50)
    k10 <- cl / v1
    k12 <- q / v1
    k21 <- q / v2
    d/dt(depot) <- -ka * depot
    d/dt(cent) <- ka * depot - (k10 + k12) * cent + k21 * peri
    d/dt(peri) <- k12 * cent - k21 * peri
    cp <- 1000 * cent / v1
    d/dt(ce) <- ke0 * (cp - ce)          # effect compartment
    resp <- 100 * ce / (ec50 + ce)       # Emax(100) response
    cp ~ lnorm(lnorm.sd)
    resp ~ add(resp.sd)
  })
}

dEff <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(id) {
  rbind(data.frame(ID = id, TIME = 0, DV = NA_real_, AMT = 100, EVID = 1,
                   CMT = "depot"),
        data.frame(ID = id, TIME = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12),
                   DV = c(15, 22, 24, 18, 12, 8), AMT = 0, EVID = 0,
                   CMT = "cp"),
        data.frame(ID = id, TIME = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24),
                   DV = c(10, 25, 40, 35, 25, 12), AMT = 0, EVID = 0,
                   CMT = "resp"))
}))
codeEff <- portCheck(effCpt, dEff)

Both endpoints ride the same solve; likInner0 sums the per-endpoint terms, and the analytic gradients flow through the same linkage. Note that the two residual models are different families (lognormal on concentration, additive on response) and both are ordinary ini({}) parameters with their own priors:

cat(grep("lnorm_sd|resp_sd", strsplit(codeEff$code, "\n")[[1]], value = TRUE),
    sep = "\n")
#>   real<lower=0> lnorm_sd;
#>   real<lower=0> resp_sd;
#>   theta[8] = lnorm_sd;
#>   theta[9] = resp_sd;
#>   lnorm_sd ~ cauchy(0, 1);
#>   resp_sd ~ cauchy(0, 5);

IOV

Torsten “supports” IOV the way it supports everything: you write it – occasion-level etas declared as extra parameters, constrained by hand to share one variance, and added into the occasion’s parameters. nlmixr2bayes has first-class syntax for the same structure – iov.x ~ v | occ declares one shared IOV magnitude across occasions:

iov <- function() {
  ini({
    lcl <- log(10)
    lv <- log(35)
    prior(lcl) ~ dnorm(log(10), 0.5)
    lnorm.sd <- c(0, 0.2)
    prior(lnorm.sd) ~ dcauchy(0, 1)
    eta.cl ~ 0.06       # IIV
    iov.cl ~ 0.02 | OCC # IOV: one shared magnitude across occasions
  })
  model({
    cl <- exp(lcl + eta.cl + iov.cl)
    v <- exp(lv)
    cp <- linCmt()
    cp ~ lnorm(lnorm.sd)
  })
}

dIov <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, function(id) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(occ) {
    t0 <- (occ - 1) * 24
    rbind(data.frame(ID = id, TIME = t0, DV = NA_real_, AMT = 1000, EVID = 1,
                     OCC = occ),
          data.frame(ID = id, TIME = t0 + c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12),
                     DV = c(20, 25, 18, 10, 6), AMT = 0, EVID = 0, OCC = occ))
  }))
}))
codeIov <- portCheck(iov, dIov)

Under the hood, nlmixr2est’s preprocessing hook expands iov.cl into per-occasion etas with variance fixed to one, and a single estimated sd theta carries the IOV magnitude – the same construction a Torsten user would otherwise hand-write (a unit-variance parameter scaled by a shared SD), except emitted for you and FD-verified end to end. The expansion is visible in the generated parameter block, where the IOV magnitude appears as an ordinary theta:

cat(grep("iov", strsplit(codeIov$code, "\n")[[1]], value = TRUE,
         ignore.case = TRUE), sep = "\n")
#>   real<lower=0> iov_cl;
#>   matrix[N, 1] z_rx_iov_cl_1;
#>   matrix[N, 1] z_rx_iov_cl_2;
#>   theta[4] = iov_cl;
#>   matrix[1,1] L_rx_iov_cl_1 = [[1]];
#>   eta[, 2:2] = z_rx_iov_cl_1 * L_rx_iov_cl_1';
#>   matrix[1,1] L_rx_iov_cl_2 = [[1]];
#>   eta[, 3:3] = z_rx_iov_cl_2 * L_rx_iov_cl_2';
#>   iov_cl ~ cauchy(0, 0.353553390593275);
#>   to_vector(z_rx_iov_cl_1) ~ std_normal();
#>   to_vector(z_rx_iov_cl_2) ~ std_normal();
#>   omegaOut[2:2, 2:2] = L_rx_iov_cl_1 * L_rx_iov_cl_1';
#>   omegaOut[3:3, 3:3] = L_rx_iov_cl_2 * L_rx_iov_cl_2';

The linked likelihood never sees anything but ordinary subject-level etas: the expansion happens before the Stan program is generated, so no upstream likelihood change was needed to support it.

What does not carry over

  • Torsten’s single-patient examples (pk2cpt and friends) carry over directly: a no-eta model generates a theta-only program with target += nlmixr2_pop_ll(theta) (nlmixr2est’s nlm path – the likelihood and analytic theta gradients on the natural scale). The pk2cpt port is the population port above minus the etas, with Torsten’s lognormal priors verbatim:
pk2cpt <- function() {
  ini({
    lcl <- log(10); lq <- log(15); lv1 <- log(35); lv2 <- log(105)
    lka <- log(2.5)
    prior(lcl) ~ dnorm(log(10), 0.25)
    prior(lq) ~ dnorm(log(15), 0.5)
    prior(lv1) ~ dnorm(log(35), 0.25)
    prior(lv2) ~ dnorm(log(105), 0.5)
    prior(lka) ~ dnorm(log(2.5), 1)
    lnorm.sd <- c(0, 0.2)
    prior(lnorm.sd) ~ dcauchy(0, 1)
  })
  model({
    cl <- exp(lcl); q <- exp(lq); v <- exp(lv1); vp <- exp(lv2)
    ka <- exp(lka)
    cp <- linCmt()
    cp ~ lnorm(lnorm.sd)
  })
}

d1 <- rbind(data.frame(ID = 1, TIME = 0, DV = NA_real_, AMT = 1000, EVID = 1),
            data.frame(ID = 1, TIME = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24),
                       DV = c(15, 22, 24, 18, 12, 8, 3), AMT = 0, EVID = 0))
code1 <- portCheck(pk2cpt, d1)
cat(grep("nlmixr2_pop_ll", strsplit(code1$code, "\n")[[1]], value = TRUE),
    sep = "\n")
#>   real nlmixr2_pop_ll(vector theta);
#>   target += nlmixr2_pop_ll(theta);

That single external scalar is the whole difference: with no etas there is nothing to marginalize, so nlmixr2est’s nlm path hands Stan the complete data log-likelihood and its analytic theta gradient in one call. The tier-0 target is verified against a hand-written density with FD-checked gradients.

  • Torsten’s pmx_solve_group_* MPI parallelism distributes subjects across processes; nlmixr2bayes parallelizes subjects with OpenMP threads inside each likelihood call (cores) – same axis, different mechanics, no user-visible model difference.

  • Conversely, rxode2 capabilities with no Torsten equivalent flow through est="stan" unchanged: the censoring machinery (M2/M3/M4), the residual-error catalog, transit-compartment helpers, mu-referenced covariate handling, and delay differential equations – delay() / past() need no special handling here, because the Stan program only ever sees the linked likelihood, and rxode2 has already switched to a dense solver behind it (vignette("rxstan-dde", "nlmixr2bayes") works the same example both ways).

A note on completeness

These ports are verified at the code level – each generates a program stanc accepts, which is exactly what the chunks above did – but they have not been run against Torsten’s own example datasets, which ship inside the Torsten repository as R dump files rather than in any R package. The synthetic event tables above exercise generation, not agreement.

To reproduce a port against the original data, load Torsten’s dump and reshape the NONMEM-style vectors into the event-table columns nlmixr2 expects:

e <- new.env()
source(file.path(torstenDir, "example-models/poppk2cpt/poppk2cpt.data.R"),
       local = e)
d <- with(e, data.frame(ID = rep(seq_len(nSubjects),
                                 times = end - start + 1),
                        TIME = time, AMT = amt, EVID = evid, CMT = cmt,
                        RATE = rate, II = ii, ADDL = addl, SS = ss,
                        DV = NA_real_))
d$DV[e$iObs] <- e$cObs
fit := nlmixr2est::nlmixr2(poppk2cpt, d, est = "nuts",
                           control = nutsControl(seed = 42))

That chunk is the only one on this page that does not run when the vignette is built – torstenDir has to point at a clone of the Torsten repository.
